extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners learning Coq for practical software verification
extracted.subtask_description: An introductory tutorial on using the Coq proof assistant for defining inductive types and relations, writing functions (fixpoints), and proving properties using tactics; includes worked examples (board game, lists, Needham–Schroeder protocol) and guidance on recursion/termination and extraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructors are injective and distinct
rubrics_metrics.description: The constructors of an inductive type are injective and distinct (e.g., S n = S m → n = m and S n ≠ 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These lemmas are part of the standard library for nat but must be proved for new inductive types; tactics exist to automate proving such contradictions/equalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use discriminate to exploit constructor-distinctness
rubrics_metrics.description: discriminate H will prove any goal if H is a proof of t1 = t2 with t1 and t2 starting with different constructors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With no argument discriminate will try to find such a contradiction in the context. Example: discriminate H solves S (S n) = 1 contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use injection to exploit constructor-injectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: injection H assumes H is a proof of t1 = t2 with t1 and t2 starting with the same constructor and deduces equalities between corresponding subterms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It will add equalities u1 = u2, v1 = v2, ... as new hypotheses. Example: injection H yields n = S m from S n = S (S m).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive propositions represent logical connectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositional connectives (except negation, implication and ∀) are declared using inductive definitions: False has no constructors, True has one proof I, conjunction corresponds to product type, disjunction to inductive with two constructors, existentials and equality are also inductively defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can Print and Check these inductive propositions (e.g., Print False, Print or, Check or_ind) to see their induction/elimination principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit vs implicit type arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: The Coq kernel requires explicit type arguments for polymorphic constructors/constructs, but you can ask Coq to infer them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Set Implicit Arguments to tell Coq to infer type arguments when possible; use Implicit Arguments name [args] to set implicit arguments for a specific object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use notation to make constructors readable
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce notations to make compound constructors more readable (e.g. Notation "[ x | y | z ]" := (Triple x y z)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notations help reuse functions and make inputs closer to intended surface syntax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern-matching syntax and coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Pattern-matching uses 'match term with c1 args1 ⇒ term1 ... cn argsn ⇒ termn end' where patterns are examined sequentially and must cover the whole domain of the inductive type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patterns may be nested and contain the universal pattern; generalized pattern-matching compiles to primitive patterns. Equivalent surface constructs: let (...) := t in u for single-constructor types and if t then u1 else u2 for two-constructor booleans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only structural recursion (Fixpoint) is allowed by default
rubrics_metrics.description: General fixpoints are disallowed because they lead to unsoundness; only structural recursion is accepted: each recursive call must be on a term structurally smaller than the chosen recursive argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'Fixpoint name (args){struct xi} : type := term' where xi is the recursive argument; if {struct xi} is omitted the system will attempt to infer it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixpoint syntax enforces decreasing argument discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: The declared type of the fixpoint is forall (x1:type1)...type and occurrences of name in term must be applied to at least i arguments and the i-th must be structurally smaller than xi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can define multiple variants (recursing on different arguments) as long as each recursive call decreases the specified structural argument (examples: plus1 and plus2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Syntactic restrictions on fixpoint declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: There are strong syntactic restrictions: there should be one decreasing argument per fixpoint; Coq may reject definitions if it cannot guess a decreasing argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If needed, refactor recursion using higher-order functions, local let fix, or well-founded recursion to express more complex recursive schemes (e.g., Ackermann via nested let fix).

rubrics_metrics.name: Computation behaviour of fixpoints and simplification
rubrics_metrics.description: A fixpoint can be computed when the recursive argument starts with a constructor; simpl simplifies fixpoint definitions applied to constructors; simpl name simplifies only the named fixpoint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equations corresponding to fixpoint definitions are not always solved by reflexivity — they may require case analysis or destruct on the recursive argument; recommended to prove defining equations and use rewrite in a controlled way when full simplification is too aggressive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empty inductive types imply proof irrelevance consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Coq allows empty inductive data-types; there are no closed values of such types, but one can write functions from that empty type to any type and prove False from an hypothesis of that empty type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Inductive E : Set := Ei. Fixpoint Eany A x : A := match x with (Ei y) => Eany A y end. From x : E one can derive False.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Eval compute to inspect normal forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'Eval compute in term.' to reduce terms and print normal forms (examples: arithmetic, function application, triple_map results).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful to check expected computational behaviour of definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use List library and established notations for list algorithms
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent arrays by functional lists and import List/ZArith; use standard notations (a::l, l1++l2) and library functions (skipn, In) when proving algorithms on lists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define sum and max by Fixpoint; when pattern-matching is non-elementary, prove auxiliary equations (e.g., max_cons) to facilitate rewriting and proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify function behavior via inductive predicates or equations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use predicates (e.g., In) or equational properties (sum nil=0, sum (a::l)=a+sum l) as functional specifications for correctness proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the correctness property (e.g., sum_max_prop) and prove by induction and simplification plus arithmetic reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: All functions in Coq must terminate
rubrics_metrics.description: Termination is enforced by Coq; all definable functions must be provably terminating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For more sophisticated termination arguments use well-founded recursion or encode termination proofs via accessibility predicates (Acc/Event) and then recurse on those proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define inductive relations by closure properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Inductive definitions model relations specified by closure properties (inference rules); each clause is a constructor whose type is the logical formula of the clause (e.g., LE, move, moves).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coq automatically generates induction/elimination principles (e.g., LE_ind) capturing minimality; there are often multiple equivalent implementations and choices affect ease of proofs (use parameters to factor out common args).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer parameterizing inductive definitions for proof convenience
rubrics_metrics.description: Making arguments parameters (rather than indices) in inductive definitions often simplifies subsequent proofs; different encodings are possible and the choice impacts proof difficulty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: two encodings of ≤ on nat differ; factor out n as a parameter when helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model complex state via nested inductive types
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent structured state (e.g., 3×3 board) by nested inductive/polymorphic types (triple (triple color)), and define operations (turn_row/turn_col) via reusable functions (triple_map, triple_map_select).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Notation and Set Implicit Arguments to keep surface syntax concise; define move relations either with logical connectives (exists) or as direct inductive relations to suit proof style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define reflexive-transitive closure as an inductive relation
rubrics_metrics.description: To define reachability, introduce an inductive relation for reflexive-transitive closure with constructors for step and init (moves_step, moves_init).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove simple lemmas (move_moves) by applying the inductive constructors; prove reachability by sequencing steps and using auto/replace when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent optional/partial results using option type
rubrics_metrics.description: When a function may fail to return a value, use option type (Some/None) rather than, e.g., an arbitrary default, to encode absence explicitly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: linear search returns option nat; define specification predicates (correct) to capture intended behavior and use Hint Constructors to help auto.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hint Constructors to help automation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'Hint Constructors inductive_name.' to add constructors to the auto hint database for tactic automation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This helps tactics like auto find and apply constructors for inductive predicates used in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: destruct tactic for proof by case analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: destruct t generates a subgoal per constructor of t, introducing variables/hypotheses for constructor arguments; use 'destruct t as pat' to name introduced variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the goal is ∀x:I, P then 'intros pat' will introduce x and immediately destruct it using the pattern; when more control is needed use case (more elementary).

rubrics_metrics.name: induction tactic generalizes dependent hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: induction term applies the induction principle generated for the inductive type; it generalizes dependent hypotheses of term and builds the property used in the induction from occurrences of term in the goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If only some occurrences should be abstracted, use 'pattern term at occs' first; if you need to generalize the goal before induction use 'cut' (to add a proposition) or 'generalise' for variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction on proofs vs inversion
rubrics_metrics.description: When term belongs to an inductive relation, induction uses the minimality principle. If recursion is not needed prefer inversion which exploits all information of the hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If some arguments xi are complex terms, transform the goal to ∀y, (I ... y ...) ⇒ xi = y ⇒ G and then do induction on the proof of (I ... y ...).

rubrics_metrics.name: Find invariants for proofs that cannot be done by plain induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Some proofs (e.g., showing impossibility of moves to a certain board) require finding a preserved invariant (e.g., number of white tokens in corners) and deriving contradiction from hypothesized reachability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for conserved quantities and express them as predicates to enable contradiction-based proofs rather than direct induction on a bad hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advanced inductive definitions: infinite branching and Acc
rubrics_metrics.description: Coq's inductive mechanism can express infinite branching constructors (e.g., lim : (nat -> ord) -> ord) and the accessibility predicate Acc capturing well-foundedness: Acc_intro : (forall y, R y x -> Acc R y) -> Acc R x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acc is the key to define general fixpoints/recursion on well-founded relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent types for indexed data (vectors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce types indexed by values (dependent types) to capture invariants like length: Inductive vect (A:Type): nat -> Type := v0 : vect 0 | v1 : forall n, A -> vect n -> vect (S n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dependent types allow expressing size/other invariants at the type level and can be used to ensure correctness of operations by construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model protocols with mutually inductive relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Encode distributed protocols and adversary capabilities using (possibly mutually) inductive relations for send, receive and known; messages and composition/encryption are modeled as inductive message terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parametrize protocol sections (Section Protocol; Variable X:agent) and prove lemmas formalizing desired/counterexample behaviors (e.g., Lemma flaw showing protocol failure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Partiality patterns: option, relations, subset types
rubrics_metrics.description: For partial functions choose between: (1) extend by arbitrary value (bad for polymorphic B), (2) return option B (requires case analysis), or (3) model as relation A→B→Prop and prove functionality; subset types carry preconditions in types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Option can be hidden with monadic notations; relations require introducing y and proof F x y; subset types {x:A | dom x} package the proof with the value and are useful to hide proof arguments in function calls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotated programs and proof-term overhead
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotated programs combine program and proof but contain proof-terms that can bloat printing/equality checking/reduction; Coq lacks systematic proof-irrelevance to hide these.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Program and type classes to separate programming from proof obligations when possible; use extraction to remove proof artifacts for executable code.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use extraction to obtain executable OCaml/Haskell code
rubrics_metrics.description: Coq's extraction mechanism removes proof-related parts and outputs equivalent OCaml or Haskell programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extraction gives back the expected recursive implementations (example: findP extraction yields a simple recursive OCaml function matching the intended algorithm).

rubrics_metrics.name: Model loops / non-structural recursion via Event or well-founded recursion
rubrics_metrics.description: Encode termination proofs via inductive predicates (Event P n) to represent 'P true now or in the future', and use decidability to implement loop/find functions; more generally use well-founded relations (Fix with well_founded R) and Acc to define general recursion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct Event/Acc proofs and recurse structurally on those proofs; use Fix combinator from Coq.Init.Wf (Fix : well_founded R -> ... ) and use the provided Fix_eq to reason about the fixpoint equation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use decidability (sumbool) for constructive case-splitting
rubrics_metrics.description: sumbool {A}+{B} encodes decidable propositions carrying the witness of which disjunct holds; useful to write constructive algorithms that branch on decidable predicates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check patterns like forall n m : nat, { n <= m }+{ m < n } to express decidability of order; use Left/Right constructors in implementation and extraction yields typical if/then/else branching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design optimized algorithms with auxiliary inductive invariants
rubrics_metrics.description: To optimize algorithms (e.g., sub-linear search) introduce inductive predicates capturing input properties (decrease: successive elements do not decrease by more than 1) and use library functions (skipn) plus well-founded recursion to prove correctness and termination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define the inductive property, add 'Hint Constructors' for automation, and implement recursive functions that exploit the invariant to skip elements safely.
